A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SERA study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching. V3 removes the model-card appendix, while retaining Appendices A–D.

before.justification: V1 reports original SERA evaluations, scaling experiments, repository specialization, ablations and statistical analyses, including detailed results in the appendices.

after.justification: V3 retains these original empirical results and adds an analysis relating line-level recall to issue-resolution rates.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 changes the stated first-rollout prompt from a bug 'downstream of' the sampled function to one 'related to' it, broadening the documented instruction. The two-rollout pipeline, PR synthesis, verification rule and SFT recipe remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish regeneration of training data.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same training corpora drawn from 121 codebases, SWE-bench Verified evaluation, and Django, Sympy and Sphinx specialization. The new correlation analysis uses additional evaluations of the existing benchmark, without establishing a new task, domain or test scenario.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the leaderboard, controlled SWE-smith/BugPilot comparisons and repository-specialization experiments. The deleted model-card comparison tables repeat retained results. The new correlation plot does not introduce an identifiable new baseline comparison against SERA.

E3.justification: V3 Section 5.2 adds a validation protocol comparing average line-level recall with test-based resolution rates across 1,036 evaluations, representing over 500,000 task evaluations. Previously reported training budgets, sample sizes, context lengths and evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 5.2 and Figure 6 examine whether line-level recall tracks code correctness measured through test outcomes. This adds a focused validation analysis; the existing verification, truncation, filtering, reasoning-removal and rollout-mixing ablations are retained.

E5.justification: V3 adds a correlation estimate without an accompanying confidence interval. It removes statements that ANOVA assumptions were met for specialization and rollout mixing, and the normality violation motivating the verification Kruskal–Wallis test. Existing test statistics, three-seed reporting and standard deviations remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Figure 6 newly reports a recall–resolution correlation of r=0.898. Figure 1 replaces the claim that general data matches the teacher at 25,000 samples with a 3.5-fold efficiency gap by failure to match at twice the specialized sample count, consistent with Section 4.3. Numerical entries in Tables 1–15 are unchanged; Appendix D drops the 4.8-fold raw-compute comparison with SkyRL.

T1.justification: The SVG equations, patch-recall definition, scaling-law formulation and inverse cost calculation are unchanged. V3 adds empirical correlation evidence, without new mathematical definitions, theoretical results or proofs.

C1.justification: The headline contributions remain efficient SFT-based coding agents, generation without unit-test verification, competitive fully open performance and inexpensive repository specialization. The abstract is reorganized, but its scientific claims and the reported 26-fold and 57-fold cost advantages are retained.

C2.justification: V3 interprets the new correlation as supporting line-level recall as a continuous, inexpensive correctness proxy applicable to any codebase. It also qualifies rollout mixing from 'without degrading performance' to 'little to no performance degradation.' The main limitations concerning benchmark scope, private repositories and model generalization remain.

D1.justification: Removing Appendix E loses explicit installation and launch commands, individual model identifiers, startup timing and Apache 2.0 license information. Core hyperparameters, deployment hardware guidance and code/data links remain. The CLI repository link moves to the first page, rather than becoming newly available.

R1.justification: The reference lists contain the same works, and the positioning against synthetic-data pipelines, reinforcement learning and agent scaffolds is substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: V3 reorganizes the abstract, makes localized language edits, corrects cross-references and removes the unresolved 'Appendix ??' reference. It inserts Section 5.2, renumbers subsequent ablations and deletes the model-card appendix, while preserving the main narrative structure.

P2.justification: V3 adds the correlation scatterplot as Figure 6; the retained truncation plot becomes Figure 7. Figures and tables are repositioned, Figure 1's caption is corrected, and appendix table captions move above their tables. Model-card Tables 16–19 disappear, including duplicated performance displays.

improvement.justification: The added recall analysis provides a useful, limited empirical check, and the corrected Figure 1 caption resolves an inconsistency with Section 4.3. These modest gains are partly offset by lost deployment, licensing and statistical-assumption details. The new aggregate correlation lacks model-selection details and does not establish individual-patch correctness, so it supports only a limited improvement in scientific evidence and clarity.
